newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan says Israel pushes peace process to crisis.
newsitem.headline: Jordan says Israel pushes peace process to crisis.

text.p: Jordanian Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti said on Tuesday unilateral Israeli decisions on Jewish settlements and a limited West Bank pullback had pushed the Middle East peace process into crisis.
Speaking after talks with Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, Kabariti urged Israel "to resort to the negotiating table and not to dictate facts."
"We believe the peace process is passing through a very real crisis," Kabariti told reporters, echoing remarks by Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat.
"If we are not to talk about justice and if we are not to talk about confidence and trust then I don't think there is a meaning for the peace process."

Kabariti said King Hussein had sent two letters to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stating Jordan's opposition to plans to build 6,500 Jewish homes in Arab East Jerusalem at Jabal Abu Ghoneim, known by Israel as Har Homa, and its decision to withdraw from just nine percent of West Bank territory.

Israeli newspapers reported on Tuesday that the king said he didn't have "an ounce of trust" in Netanyahu. The Israeli leader, visiting Moscow, was quoted by Israeli army radio as retorting that King Hussein's comments were unbalanced.
Mordechai sought to play down the icy exchanges between the Netanyahu and the Jordanian monarch, seen as Israel's closest Arab friend when Jordan signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994.
"I am sure they will find a way to negotiate. There are some misunderstandings but I am sure we can overcome those problems," he said. "Both of them are honest and respect each other."
But Kabariti, who pointedly declined to appear in public with the Israeli general, said his government was not impressed with Israel's justifications for its moves.

"I affirmed to the Israeli minister that Israel, with its unilateral decisions, either over settlements or on the scale of the redeployment, has put the Palestinians in a great predicament, whose results (the Palestinians) have to bear alone," Kabariti said. "Jordan rejects these decisions."

"No matter what the reasoning of the Israeli government regarding Abu Ghoneim and regarding the implementation of the redeployment, we don't think we have got satisfactory answers," he said before leaving for parliament, where Islamist deputies planned to call for the 1994 peace treaty to be abrogated.

Kabariti said King Hussein would push the issue when he goes to the United States on Friday for talks with President Bill Clinton. The king's visit follows trips by Netanyahu, Arafat, and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.
He warned Israel that Palestinian authorities could not be accountable for any outburst of anger when construction starts on the Jewish homes in East Jerusalem.
"They cannot expect the Palestinians to work as policemen for their bulldozers when they move into Abu Ghoneim," Kabariti said.
Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed in clashes last September after Netanyahu opened a new entrance to an archaeology tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem.
